nearby_not_selected.description: When two named participants explicitly agree to do a shared activity at a stated time (e.g., 'let's paint next Saturday' / 'Sounds good'), extract a single candidate with both participants, the activity, and the exact time.
content: Only when a proposal is met with a clear explicit agreement, extract a joint plan/event candidate naming BOTH participants, the shared activity, and the agreed time exactly as stated; do not compute or guess a calendar date.
Preserve the mutual commitment as one fact; do not split into separate per-subject candidates. Do not apply when only one person expresses interest or when no time is stated.

nearby_not_selected.name: Attribute first-person narrated events to the speaker
nearby_not_selected.description: When a chat message narrates an event in first person ('I...', 'we...'), even if it opens by addressing another participant ('Hey Deborah...'), bind the event to the message's speaker. Not for third-person statements or unidentified speakers.
content: When a message narrates an event in first person, set the extracted memory's subject to the message's speaker from metadata, never to the addressee or someone merely greeted. If 'we' is used, keep the group as stated. Do not apply to third-person statements.
If speaker metadata is missing or the first-person referent is ambiguous, SKIP extraction instead of guessing a subject.

When a first-person narration includes a relative time phrase ('last night', 'yesterday'), store the resolved absolute date from the message timestamp AND the original wording. Only when timing is explicitly stated; never invent a date.

When a first-person narration places the speaker in a named place (event, past trip, comparative reply, or exploration), extract the visit/presence fact with person, place, and stated time; preserve exact wording and qualifiers. Do not apply to hypothetical, wish, third-party, or not-yet-visited places; a future scheduled event should be extracted as a future event, never as a past visit. Keep any stated preference/liking for the place as a separate memory; do not merge it into the visit fact or imply the person has visited when only future travel is stated. When the same visit is already recorded, prefer UPDATE/MERGE over duplicate ADD; if no date is stated, leave date unset without inventing one.

When a first-person narration names a location for the speaker's own action, attach the place to the speaker's presence (e.g., 'Tim was in California and had a chat with a fan'), not to a secondary person or object. Do NOT apply when the location modifies another entity ('my friend in California'), the interaction was explicitly remote, or the place is only a future wish. If ambiguous ('a chat with a fan in California'), preserve original wording; do not assert speaker presence or create a travel/location memory. During CRUD, update an existing event memory to include the speaker's presence only if the source message supports it; otherwise leave unchanged.

nearby_not_selected.name: Extract explicit self-disclosed preferences separately
nearby_not_selected.description: When a message contains an explicit first-person statement of liking, loving, preferring, or a favorite (e.g., 'I love...', 'my favorite is...'), during extraction create a preference candidate for each named item.
content: Scan every message for explicit preference signals such as 'favorite', 'love', 'like', 'prefer', 'enjoy', or 'one of my favorites'; create a preference candidate when present.
Record each distinct liked item in its own candidate, preserving exact item name and all modifiers (e.g., 'dairy-free chocolate mousse'), plus relational context like 'besides X' if stated.
If the same turn also contains an event such as recommending or sharing, emit both a preference memory and an event memory; do not let the event subsume the preference.

nearby_not_selected.name: Preserve health event context
nearby_not_selected.description: When extracting event memories, if a user message narrates a health scare, medical visit, hospital stay, or check-up outcome, preserve the specific triggering context along with the resolution.
content: When extracting a health/medical event from a user message, capture both the triggering context (e.g., 'during a medical check-up', 'at the ER', 'after a test') and the resolution (e.g., 'turned out to be a misunderstanding'). Do not reduce the event to only hospitalization or final verdict.

If the message separates trigger from outcome, include both clauses in the candidate content to keep the full sequence (e.g., 'found something suspicious during a check-up, which turned out to be a misunderstanding').
For health event memories, preserve the precise setting over the emotional reaction, because the setting distinguishes multiple health events for the same person.

nearby_not_selected.name: Preserve euphemistic death/loss implications
nearby_not_selected.description: When a message describes a person as no longer alive via euphemistic or indirect phrasing (e.g., 'will never be able to...', 'I miss him here', 'passed away'), during extraction preserve the exact wording and the implied fact that the person is deceased.
content: Preserve exact euphemistic phrasing when it implies death/permanent absence (e.g., 'will never be able to...', 'I miss him here', 'passed away', 'I lost him'). Record that the person is no longer alive.
Do not paraphrase away the loss meaning (e.g., write 'a friend who will never be able to support me; I miss him here' rather than 'a friend who will never support her').
Never invent specifics not stated (cause/date of death, exact relationship); keep the speaker's words and certainty.
At CRUD time, add/update the memory to include the death/loss implication whenever it is stated or clearly implied; skip when no loss/death implication exists.

selected.name: Attribute first-person narrated events to the speaker
selected.description: When a chat message narrates an event in first person ('I...', 'we...'), even if it opens by addressing another participant ('Hey Deborah...'), bind the event to the message's speaker. Not for third-person statements or unidentified speakers.
content: When a message narrates an event in first person, set the extracted memory's subject to the message's speaker from metadata, never to the addressee or someone merely greeted. If 'we' is used, keep the group as stated. Do not apply to third-person statements.
If speaker metadata is missing or the first-person referent is ambiguous, SKIP extraction instead of guessing a subject.

When a first-person narration includes a relative time phrase ('last night', 'yesterday'), store the resolved absolute date from the message timestamp AND the original wording. Only when timing is explicitly stated; never invent a date.

When a first-person narration places the speaker in a named place (event, past trip, comparative reply, or exploration), extract the visit/presence fact with person, place, and stated time; preserve exact wording and qualifiers. Do not apply to hypothetical, wish, third-party, or not-yet-visited places; a future scheduled event should be extracted as a future event, never as a past visit. Keep any stated preference/liking for the place as a separate memory; do not merge it into the visit fact or imply the person has visited when only future travel is stated. When the same visit is already recorded, prefer UPDATE/MERGE over duplicate ADD; if no date is stated, leave date unset without inventing one.

When a first-person narration names a location for the speaker's own action, attach the place to the speaker's presence (e.g., 'Tim was in California and had a chat with a fan'), not to a secondary person or object. Do NOT apply when the location modifies another entity ('my friend in California'), the interaction was explicitly remote, or the place is only a future wish. If ambiguous ('a chat with a fan in California'), preserve original wording; do not assert speaker presence or create a travel/location memory. During CRUD, update an existing event memory to include the speaker's presence only if the source message supports it; otherwise leave unchanged.

This skill is specifically designed for such cases and would materially change extraction by correctly attributing events to the speaker.
